description: We are a team of curious minds, passionate problem-solvers, and aspiring innovators united by a shared interest in space exploration, science, and technology. Through the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to combine creativity, collaboration, and software development to make the wonders of our universe more accessible to everyone. We are excited to explore astronomical data, experiment with new ideas, and build an interactive solution that inspires curiosity about the cosmos. For us, this is more than a hackathon—it's an opportunity to learn, push boundaries, and contribute to a future where technology brings us closer to understanding the universe.
summary: Earth System Trend Detective is a web app that lets anyone test whether an environmental change is real or just noise. Pick any place on an OpenStreetMap map and a variable (temperature, rainfall, humidity, sunlight or soil wetness). The app fetches 45 years of NASA POWER data, measures the trend with Sen's slope, and tests it with the Mann–Kendall test. It then stress-tests the result: a heatmap shows whether the verdict holds or collapses when you change the start and end years. It also checks the answer against ERA5, an independent European dataset. A plain-language case file gives a verdict, a confidence label and honest limits. It also shows the real size of the data grid cell and which towns it covers. Guided cases from Ghana and the Sahel show the method at work: Accra warming at about 0.18 °C per decade, confirmed by both datasets and two nearby cities whose rainfall trends diverge in NASA's data but barely in ERA5. We also check our statistics against an independent reference and NASA's global temperature record. Climate charts are everywhere, but most people cannot tell a robust trend from a cherry-picked one. This tool makes that judgement visible, testable and shareable.
details:
What it does?
You choose a place and an environmental variable. The app answers three questions: is there a trend, is it statistically credible and does the answer depend on which years you pick? It then writes a case file with a verdict, a confidence label and its limits.

How it works.

1. Monthly data for the chosen point comes from the NASA POWER API (MERRA-2 reanalysis; CERES for solar), 1981–2025.

2. It is cleaned and turned into yearly means: day-weighted and a year needs at least 10 of 12 months.

3. The trend is Sen's slope; significance is the Mann–Kendall test with tie correction.

4. The app compares the first and last ten years.

5. It reruns the test for every start/end window at least 15 years long and draws the results as a heatmap.

6. It runs a seasonal breakdown by month and by season.

7. Verdict text comes only from fixed templates tied to the confidence label (p < 0.01 strong, p < 0.05 moderate, p < 0.10 weak). A warning appears if the trend's direction flips in more than 20% of windows, and a caution if fewer than half of the windows reach the same conclusion. In compare mode, the headline also says when one place's trend depends on the years chosen or is not confirmed by ERA5.

8. A second opinion: the same test runs on ERA5, an independent reanalysis from the European Copernicus programme (via Open-Meteo), for the same years. The case file says whether the two datasets agree and warns when they do not.

9. We checked our data pipeline with NASA Giovanni: MERRA-2 air temperature for the Accra grid cell, downloaded from Giovanni, gives the same +0.182 °C per decade as NASA POWER, with yearly values within 0.002 °C.

10. OpenStreetMap shows where the data comes from. The map outlines the actual grid cell, and Overpass lists the towns inside it. This makes clear that the data is a regional average, not a single weather station.

Benefits.
A two-minute guided tour walks first-time users through every panel. People can check claims about climate change themselves. The tool teaches why the choice of start year matters and always says "trend", never "cause". It is free, needs no login or key, works on a phone, and supports keyboard and screen-reader use with colour-blind-safe charts.

What we hope to achieve.
A tool that teachers, students, journalists and local planners in Ghana and beyond can use to separate robust environmental change from noise.

Tools.
JavaScript (Vite, MapLibre GL for the 3D globe, Leaflet, Chart.js), Vitest for 51 unit tests, and Python (pymannkendall) to generate reference results. Hosted as a static site with no backend.
